name: Caffeine shampoo

card.summary: Marketed anti-hair-loss shampoo (Alpecin and others); one women's trial exists, with little else behind it.
card.note: Evidence in the sources reviewed is a single study in women; results were not available.

quick.overview:
Caffeine shampoos are cosmetic products sold to slow thinning hair, with Alpecin the best-known brand. They are used as a scalp wash rather than a drug.

The only study found examined a phyto-caffeine shampoo in women with female androgenetic alopecia; its results were not available, and no men-specific trial was found.
quick.mechanism: Marketing and study background describe caffeine as promising in vitro and in vivo for androgenetic alopecia; the sources reviewed do not detail the proposed mechanism.
quick.risks: No safety information was available in the sources reviewed. These are sold as cosmetic products rather than approved hair-loss drugs.

lead: Caffeine shampoo is a rinse-off cosmetic shampoo that contains caffeine and is marketed to people with thinning hair, aiming to keep more hair on the head and make hair look and feel thicker. The best-known brand is Alpecin, a German shampoo line for men whose maker says its caffeine content can help reduce hair loss [1]. The idea is that caffeine applied to the scalp may work against the effects of androgens on hair follicles, and users wash with it as part of a routine alongside treatments such as minoxidil or finasteride [2][3].

A 2020 study in the Giornale Italiano di Dermatologia e Venereologia tested a cosmetic phyto-caffeine shampoo in women with androgenetic alopecia in a single-centre, double-blind, randomised, parallel trial against a control shampoo over six months. The phyto-caffeine group had significantly fewer hairs pulled in a hair-pull test than the control group (-3.1 versus -0.5 hairs), improved on hair loss intensity and hair strength, and both products were well tolerated [4]. A 2019 review in the International Journal of Cosmetic Science described caffeine as the most studied phytochemical for hair loss and said the studies offer reasonable evidence that, when dosed adequately for long enough, caffeine reaches the follicle at levels that could ameliorate hair loss in some patients [1].

In March 2018 the UK Advertising Standards Authority ruled that Alpecin could no longer say in UK ads that it helps reduce hair loss, finding the evidence the company had submitted (eight full studies, several summaries and a consumer survey) inadequate [1].

chain: Caffeine-containing shampoo is lathered on the scalp
Caffeine is proposed to counter androgen effects on follicles
Less shedding and thicker-looking, stronger hair
angle.text: People use caffeine shampoo as a daily or regular scalp wash with the aim of reducing shedding and keeping hair looking fuller. The one trial found measured fewer hairs pulled and greater hair strength in women with androgenetic alopecia.

infobox: ASA, March 2018: 'helps reduce hair loss' claim not allowed

paras: Caffeine shampoos are rinse-off scalp products with caffeine as an active cosmetic ingredient. The 2020 trial abstract describes androgenetic alopecia as the most common type of hair loss in both sexes, affecting up to 57 percent of women by age 80, and as carrying a heavy psychological burden, which it gives as background for testing caffeine-based products [4].

Alpecin is a German shampoo brand for men, said by Wikipedia to have been established in 1905 (its infobox gives 1930 as the introduction date) [1]. It has sponsored professional cycling teams, including Team Giant-Alpecin from 2015, Katusha-Alpecin from 2017 to 2019 and Alpecin-Fenix from 2020 [1].

The manufacturer publishes its supporting studies on its website while noting it cannot guarantee their accuracy [1]. The 2018 UK ASA ruling concluded that the claim that Alpecin helps reduce hair loss was misleading for lack of adequate scientific evidence [1].

On T Nation, users describe caffeine shampoo as an add-on: one poster says using Nizoral and Alpecin together made hair look and feel thicker within a week [5]; another says a caffeine shampoo is the only thing they use against hair loss while considering an oral steroid [6]. A poster discussing compounds for facial hair says hair-loss shampoos with biotin and caffeine seemed to make their beard and body hair hairier but did nothing for actual thinning [7]. Posts discussing hair loss regimens typically place shampoos alongside the so-called big three of minoxidil, finasteride and ketoconazole [8]. A Hacker News item also links a podcast asking whether caffeine hair products like Alpecin stimulate hair growth [9].

The 2020 randomised trial in female androgenetic alopecia reported significantly fewer hairs pulled with the phyto-caffeine shampoo than control at six months, with improvements on most secondary measures and good tolerability [4]. The 2019 International Journal of Cosmetic Science review discussed the follicle-level evidence for caffeine [1]. No men-specific trial of a caffeine shampoo was found.

timeline.event: UK ASA bars the Alpecin claim that it helps reduce hair loss. [1]
International Journal of Cosmetic Science review calls caffeine the most studied phytochemical for hair loss. [1]
Randomised trial of a phyto-caffeine shampoo in women with androgenetic alopecia published. [4]

lore.intro: Forum users mention caffeine shampoo as a low-effort adjunct to minoxidil and finasteride and to hormone-therapy hair-loss worries [5][6][8].

claims.believers: A T Nation poster using Alpecin with Nizoral said hair looked and felt thicker than a week earlier [5].
claims.experts: One six-month double-blind trial in women found fewer hairs pulled with a phyto-caffeine shampoo than control [4]; the UK ASA found the evidence for the brand's hair-loss claim inadequate [1].

claims.claim: Caffeine shampoo can offset hair loss from anabolic steroid or hormone therapy
claims.believers: A T Nation poster asked about acne and hair loss with oral anabolic steroids said they use only caffeine shampoo for hair loss [6].
claims.experts: No studies of caffeine shampoo in hormone-therapy-related hair loss were found.

claims.claim: Hair-loss shampoos with caffeine and biotin make beard and body hair thicker
claims.believers: One T Nation poster reported hairier beard and body hair from such shampoos [7].
claims.experts: No studies of caffeine shampoo on beard or body hair were found.
